overview: Yanomami communities live across the forested upper Amazon and Orinoco region in Brazil and Venezuela. The name embraces related peoples and languages, including Sanöma and Ninam. The imported 1492 to 1500 outline is an approximate regional label; it cannot establish every community’s boundary in that period, and its cutoff does not mark their disappearance.

periods.title: Earlier forest histories
periods.summary: The map opens on a broad regional identity whose early borders remain uncertain.

periods.title: Movement and expanding contact
periods.summary: Communities expanded from the Parima region; later missions and government posts intensified outside contact.

periods.title: Roads and mining invasions
periods.summary: Road construction and expanding mining brought disease and territorial disruption.

periods.title: Recognised territory and continuing peoples
periods.summary: Brazil recognised the Indigenous territory; communities continue defending it and producing knowledge.

items.text: Oral histories and early documents identify the Serra Parima as an important historical centre. Movement toward surrounding lowlands probably accelerated in the early nineteenth century. Exchange with neighbouring peoples helped bring new crops and metal tools before regular direct encounters with Brazilian officials or missionaries.

From the 1940s into the 1960s, missions and government posts made outside contact more regular. They supplied manufactured goods and sometimes medical help, but also became sources of measles, influenza and whooping-cough outbreaks. A new trading connection could bring a dangerous new infection.

Construction of the Perimetral Norte road began in 1973. Communities near its workers suffered infectious disease, while mineral surveys and mining invasions drew outsiders deeper into the forest. The late 1980s brought particularly intense mining pressure, damaging both community health and the land that supplied food.

Brazil recognised the Terra Indígena Yanomami in 1992, covering about 96,650 square kilometres in Amazonas and Roraima. This Brazilian legal territory is only part of the wider cross-border homeland. It is also home to Ye’kwana, a distinct people whose language belongs to the Karib family.

A UNICEF teaching portrait of a boy named Kiko describes a large circular communal house. Each family had its own cooking fire and hammock space, opening toward a shared centre. An opening in the roof let smoke escape. Several households could have their own corners under one enormous roof.

In the same portrait, a propped-up blackboard marked a new classroom inside the house. Kiko learned fishing, food gathering and beadwork from people around him, and attended afternoon language lessons. Reading his own language and Portuguese joined skills learned through everyday participation.

The Smithsonian catalogues a 1974 film, made from a 1971 project, in which a village headman weaves a cotton hammock while his wife and infant watch. This small domestic scene preserves patient craftwork and family company, a useful reminder that historical records can show ordinary afternoons as well as conflicts.

Women at Maturacá helped researchers identify the fungus Marasmius yanomami, whose shiny black strands decorate baskets. Their association Kumirãyôma documented collecting and using it in a bilingual book with research partners. Something that looks like dark thread can be part of a fungus: forest knowledge becomes visible in a basket.

Hutukara’s 2025 basket catalogue distinguishes different jobs and forms: women make elongated baskets for travelling or storing food, while Sanöma men make certain tubular kitchen utensils and sieves. Baskets sent for sale through the association help obtain goods requested by communities. The catalogue describes an organised community exchange, with different crafts serving different needs.

Sanöma teachers in Awaris helped produce a 2016 book about local edible mushrooms. Many grow on decaying wood in gardens and in vegetation returning after gardens are left to regrow. The book records local names alongside scientific identifications, bringing experienced forest observers and laboratory specialists into the same conversation.

A short written sample is “Ana amopö”, the Sanöma title translated on the book’s cover as Portuguese “Cogumelos”, meaning “Mushrooms”. Sanöma is one language within the Yanomami family. This is attested modern Indigenous publishing from 2016, rather than a surviving written label from the map’s fifteenth-century snapshot.

A Fiocruz study reported in 2024 found mercury in all 287 hair samples examined from nine Ninam villages in the Alto Rio Mucajaí region. Samples had been collected in October 2022, including from children and older people. The findings document a serious local health consequence in an area affected by illegal gold mining.

In August 2025, a programme in Palimiú and Maloca Paapiú trained community participants to use drones for territorial monitoring. It combined technical practice with local knowledge and safety planning. The aim was to identify threats while reducing direct encounters with intruders, giving communities another way to watch over their forest.

ending.text: Yanomami peoples continue living across Brazil and Venezuela. Mining, disease and pressure on food supplies have caused grave harm, but the map’s 1500 endpoint is not an ending. Contemporary community publishing and territorial-monitoring initiatives show people preserving knowledge, organising collectively and defending a future on their land.
